# Optimization Baselines
Also called: Baselines, CMA-ES, Classical Optimization Baselines, Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy

## Overview
This family provides black-box optimization strategies for inverse rendering problems where the [forward rendering](#1816-per-voxel-projection-object-order.md) operator $f$ is non-differentiable or gradient computation is prohibitively expensive. Unlike gradient-based siblings that rely on automatic differentiation or [adjoint methods](#789-adjoint-method.md), these methods treat the renderer as an opaque function, minimizing a photometric loss $\mathcal{L}$ by iteratively sampling and evaluating parameter candidates [S1, unofficial]. The family is distinguished by its reliance on population-based search distributions (typically Gaussian) that adapt to the local loss landscape without explicit gradient information, offering robustness against local minima and Monte Carlo noise [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate within the standard [inverse rendering loop](#5622-optimization-loops-and-training-procedures.md) defined by [Optimization Loops and Training Procedures](5622-optimization-loops-and-training-procedures.md), minimizing a photometric loss $\mathcal{L}$ between rendered color $\hat{C}(\mathbf{r})$ and ground-truth $C(\mathbf{r})$ [G]. The core mechanism involves maintaining a search distribution $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ over the parameter space $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is the mean and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the anisotropic covariance matrix capturing correlations between parameters [S1, unofficial].

The optimization proceeds in iterations. In each iteration, $k$ candidates $\{\mathbf{x}_j\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ are drawn from the current distribution $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ [S1, unofficial]. These candidates are evaluated using the black-box renderer $f$ to compute a cost $c_j = \mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}_j), \mathbf{y}^*)$ [S1, unofficial]. The distribution parameters $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ are then updated by computing a weighted average of the candidates, ranked by their cost. Higher weights are assigned to top-scoring candidates to adapt the search distribution to the local loss landscape [S1, unofficial].

This approach inherits the ability to adapt to the local loss landscape via covariance updates and provides robustness against local minima without explicit gradient information [S1, unofficial]. The method is limited by the quadratic memory complexity of the covariance matrix, restricting it to small-to-medium sized optimization problems (up to 100 parameters) [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Feature-Guided Diffusion for Inverse Rendering](7375-feature-guided-diffusion-for-inverse-rendering.md)
A fully black-box framework combining a diffusion-based inverse prediction model with CMA-ES. It conditions the proposal distribution on dense visual features extracted from the target image, avoiding the information bottleneck of scalar loss values and mitigating mode averaging in ill-posed inverse problems.
- CMA-ES: The classical evolutionary baseline using covariance matrix adaptation. It serves as the primary reference for population-based search, adapting the Gaussian distribution to the loss landscape without auxiliary models.
- Dual Annealing: Combines simulated annealing with a local search strategy to improve convergence. It uses a standard implementation (e.g., SciPy) and does not maintain an explicit covariance matrix.
- ZeroGrads: Trains a differentiable surrogate of the black-box function’s loss landscape and uses it to derive optimization gradients. It bridges the gap between black-box and gradient-based methods by learning the gradient field.
- DiBO: A diffusion-based method that combines a diffusion prior with a learned reward proxy to sample candidates from an approximate posterior over high-performing solutions. It differs from FIDE by using a reward proxy rather than dense image features for conditioning.

## Background
The family originates from the need to solve inverse rendering problems where differentiable rendering is unavailable or unstable. CMA-ES [Hansen 2006] serves as the primary evolutionary baseline, inheriting the ability to adapt to the local loss landscape via covariance updates and providing robustness against local minima without explicit gradient information [S1, unofficial]. Dual annealing [Tsallis and Stariolo 1996] combines simulated annealing with a local search strategy to improve convergence; the standard SciPy implementation [Virtanen et al. 2020] is commonly used. From more recent methods, ZeroGrads [Fischer and Ritschel 2024] trains a differentiable surrogate of the black-box function’s loss landscape and uses it to derive optimization gradients. DiBO [Yun et al. 2025] is a diffusion-based method that combines a diffusion prior with a learned reward proxy to sample candidates from an approximate posterior over high-performing solutions. Classical Bayesian Optimization (BO) is not typically compared directly because its performance overhead is non-linear with iterations and several orders of magnitude higher than that of all other methods [S1, unofficial].
